headline: Elbit Systems: revenue up 17%, EPS up 30% and a record $33 billion backlog driven by European orders; shares rise 6%
takeaway: Revenue rose 17% to $2.25 billion and non-GAAP EPS 30% to $4.36, beating the $3.94 consensus. The order backlog reached a record $33.0 billion, three quarters of it from customers outside Israel, and free cash flow of $276 million was more than 150% of profit. The shares rose 5.9%.
results: Elbit Systems reported revenue of $2,252.1 million for the third quarter, up 17% from $1,921.6 million. GAAP net income was $177.9 million, or $3.70 a share, and non-GAAP net income $210.0 million, or $4.36 a share, against $3.35 a year earlier. Non-GAAP gross margin rose to 25.7% from 25.2%, and research and development spending was 6.5% of revenue, helped by about $20 million recognised under a new Israeli R&D incentive law.

By segment, ISTAR and electronic warfare grew 32% on high-power laser, electronic-warfare and maritime systems in Asia-Pacific and Israel; Land and Armaments grew 28% on ammunition sales in Israel; C4I and Cyber grew 11% on European command-and-control systems; Twenty-Six Defense, the renamed US subsidiary, grew 10%; and Aerospace grew 4%, as more drone sales in Israel offset fewer precision-guided munitions in Asia-Pacific.

The backlog of $33.0 billion rose mainly on European orders; about 74% comes from outside Israel and about 35% is scheduled to be delivered by the end of 2027. Nine-month operating cash flow was $862.5 million. The board declared a dividend of $1.00 a share.
mgmt: Chief executive Bezhalel Machlis said Elbit delivered high-teens revenue growth with continued margin expansion, operating profit and EPS up more than 30%, a record backlog and particularly strong free cash flow despite rising capital investment. He highlighted new AI-driven autonomous combat capabilities that coordinate multiple aerial and ground systems, and continued progress in electro-optics, guided munitions, electronic warfare and high-power lasers.

He said execution remains a priority as Elbit expands production capacity and uses AI to improve productivity. The company also noted an agreement under which it will be compensated for delayed payments by the Israeli Ministry of Defence since October 2023, and recent contracts including about $270 million for ISR and targeting payloads for an international customer.
view: Elbit has moved from being seen mainly as Israel’s wartime supplier to being one of the fastest-growing defence companies in the world, and Europe is the reason. Governments there are rebuilding stockpiles and buying artillery, air defence, drones and electronic warfare at a pace not seen since the Cold War, and Elbit offers battle-tested systems with short delivery times. The fact that the backlog grew mainly on European orders, and that three quarters of it is now international, matters because it makes Elbit less dependent on a single customer whose spending could fall after a ceasefire.

The financial quality has also improved. Margins have been inching up for several years, the cash conversion this quarter was excellent after a period when working capital tied up in Israeli government receivables weighed on cash flow, and the agreement on delayed payments should help further. High-power lasers, such as the Iron Beam system, are an area where Elbit has a genuine technological lead and could become a major export product.

The risks are political. European customers face pressure to buy European, and some governments have cancelled or paused Israeli defence contracts over the Gaza war; any broader boycott would affect the most important growth market. The shares have also re-rated sharply and trade at around 46 times trailing GAAP earnings. With a backlog equal to roughly four years of revenue, the visibility is unusual, but the valuation already reflects much of it.
watch: Watch new European contract announcements and any political pushback against Israeli suppliers, margin progress as production expands, and cash conversion in the fourth quarter.
